problem: VLM-based VLN-CE agents fine-tuned on action chunks or a single pixel-goal must infer 3D-consistent targets without any explicit 3D understanding, since VLMs are pretrained on 2D RGB conversations. A single pixel-goal gives no supervision on the interaction process (e.g. passing a sofa on the right) that produces it.
motivation: Adding depth or geometry encoders has only limited success because VLMs rarely see 3D data in pretraining. Pixel-goal supervision (InternVLA-N1, Goal2Pixel) works better by staying in the familiar 2D space. The paper argues that supervising the process, a pixel trajectory drawn near to far, is a unique 2D projection of the 3D trajectory and can act as chain-of-thought for the final goal.
key_idea: Fine-tune a VLM to autoregressively output a sequence of pixel coordinates (a trajectory from the bottom center of a down-looking image) instead of a single pixel-goal, so that trajectory generation acts as CoT for navigation.
insight: With identical data, backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, LoRA) and training, only the supervision differs: trajectory supervision beats pixel-goal supervision (R2R-CE SR 43.2 vs 39.6; RxR SR 41.54 vs 36.09). Using only the final point of the predicted trajectory as the pixel-goal also beats the pixel-goal-trained model, which supports the CoT hypothesis. Executing fewer waypoints per prediction (1 waypoint, about 0.5 m) gives the best SR, at the cost of OSR.
method: Two-stage dialogue: stage 1 outputs STOP, turn symbols (← / → = 15° each), or ↓; ↓ triggers stage 2.
Down-looking view: the agent tilts its head 30° down and captures a 640×480 image as extra input for stage 2.
Autoregressive pixel trajectory: the VLM emits normalized coordinates '[u1,v1] [u2,v2] ...' starting from the bottom center of the down-looking image, trained with plain cross-entropy.
Supervision generation: future robot base poses are projected into the current down-looking image with K and T_cur; invisible, occluded and duplicate points are filtered using depth.
Execution: predicted pixels are lifted to 3D with the depth map and the camera intrinsics/extrinsics, and the robot moves to the nearest waypoint iteratively before re-planning.
Model and history: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with the vision encoder frozen and LLM plus projector fully fine-tuned; 8 uniformly sampled history frames at 392×392.
Training data: R2R-CE + RxR-CE + ScaleVLN subset, sampled every 4 steps, 1.75M samples, one epoch.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (LLM + projector fine-tuned, vision encoder frozen); ablations use Qwen2.5-VL-7B with LoRA rank 32

results: The flagship Traj-VLN (Qwen3-VL-8B, 1.75M samples) reaches R2R-CE SR 58.4 / SPL 52.2 and RxR SR 52.6 / SPL 43.4, the best SR on both splits. It beats InternVLA-N1 (55.4 and 49.5, trained on 4.72M samples) by 3.0 and 2.9 SR and JanusVLN by 5.6 and 1.2 SR. In a matched ablation, trajectory supervision beats pixel-goal supervision by 4 and 3.29 SR.
limitations: SPL and nDTW are not the best (Goal2Pixel has SPL 52.7 on R2R-CE, SPL 44.7 and nDTW 63.0 on RxR); executing one waypoint per prediction is best for SR but costs OSR and inference frequency.
Requires a head-tilt (down-looking) view and depth to lift pixels to 3D, so it depends on a depth sensor and a specific camera setup.
Real-world evidence is only qualitative (two or three examples on a Unitree G1), and the matched ablation uses a weaker Qwen2.5-VL LoRA setup.
